cards.explanation: The answer is that Satan says he's been roaming through the earth. He came before the LORD along with the sons of God, and he doesn't name a town or a river. He says he's been “…roaming through the earth…” and walking back and forth in it. That's a big answer to a small question, like asking someone where they've been and hearing "oh, around." I like a short answer myself, but that one covers the whole planet.

The answer is integrity, friends. Speaking about Job, the LORD says, “He still retains his integrity…” He says it even after all the loss that hit Job in the first chapter (Job 1:13-19). The LORD also points out that Satan pushed Him toward ruining Job for no reason.

The answer is his flesh and bones. Satan says, “…stretch out Your hand and strike his flesh and bones…” Before this, Satan had been given power over everything Job had (Job 1:12), and now he's asking about Job's own body. He says Job “…will surely curse You to Your face.” This part of the story is a heavy one.

The answer is life, friends. The LORD says to Satan, “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life.” So there's a firm limit, and Satan has to stay inside it. Job's body is in Satan's hands, but his life isn't to be taken. Pay attention to that line, because it matters for everything that happens to Job next.

The answer is scrape. Job takes a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself as he sits among the ashes. He has terrible boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, so I think this one hurts. There's no soft towel or fancy tool in the story, only a broken piece of pottery.

The answer is that Job's wife tells him to curse God and die. She says to him, “Curse God and die!” She opens by asking whether he still retains his integrity, and then she says those words. It's a hard thing to hear, and I think it must have been a hard thing for Job to hear, too. Hold that line in your mind, friends, because Job answers her right away.

The answer is adversity. Job asks, “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” He says it to his wife, right after telling her she speaks as a foolish woman speaks. Then the text adds, “In all this, Job did not sin in what he said.” It's a short question, and it carries a lot.

The answer is False. The text says it plainly: “In all this, Job did not sin in what he said.” Satan said that Job would curse God to His face, and Job doesn't. His words stay clean even with boils from head to toe. That's a steady man, friends.

The answer is that they come to sympathize with Job and comfort him. The text says Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar met together to go and sympathize with Job and comfort him. Each of them came from his home after hearing about all the adversity that had come upon Job. They come to be with him in his suffering. That's a good reason to hit the road.

The answer is False. The text says they lifted up their eyes from afar, and they could barely recognize Job. Imagine seeing a close friend and having to look twice. I think the friends were shocked by what they saw.

The answer is that they weep aloud and tear their robes. The text says they began to weep aloud, and each man tore his robe and threw dust in the air over his head. I think they're shaken by what they see in Job. It's a heavy moment, friends, and the friends meet it with real grief.

The answer is True. The text says they sat on the ground with Job for seven days and seven nights. That's a full week of sitting there with him. It's a long time to stay put beside a friend who is hurting.

The answer is that they see how intense his suffering is. The text says no one spoke a word to him “…because they saw how intense his suffering was.” For seven days and seven nights, they just sit there with him. I think there are times when sitting close says more than talking would. It's a lesson worth knowing, friends.
